comment: Every element of the reply card that comes and goes, as opposed to the frame it lives in.
reply-card.json holds the card's configuration and its footer — the divider and the
conversation hint, which every card carries from the moment it is sent to after it has
finished — and nothing else; everything a run puts on the card and takes off it again is here.
Where each one goes is decided in FeishuCardElements, which also sets the ids the run streams
into — so a deployment replacing this file is free to restyle these elements and nothing else.
'usage' is what the turn has cost and, at the right edge of the same row, the button that
cancels the run. It is the one element here that ships with the card as the card is created:
a run is stoppable from the moment it is on screen, so the button cannot wait to be inserted,
and every card names a model in the end anyway, so the row costs the card nothing it would not
have given up later. The button is down here rather than in a row of its own under the answer
because a button under the answer is a target that moves — every word the model streams and
every panel a reader opens above it shifts it, which is how 'let me see what it read' becomes
'stop the run'. On the last line of the card it moves only with the line it shares, and it is
the only thing clickable on it. The weights are what put it beside the spend rather than out at
the right edge of the card: the first two columns are each only as wide as what they hold, and
the empty third one takes whatever is left of the row. Beside the text is where it belongs —
far right on a wide card it reads as belonging to the card rather than to the run the line is
about, and the pointer has the width of the card to travel. Weightless columns are also what
keeps the button from being stretched the way one placed straight in the card body is on
mobile. The element id lands on the button, not on the row, because the run ends by taking the
button off the card and the spend line has to outlive it. Its label is notation-sized, the
same as the spend it sits beside: the tiny button size is padding rather than type, so without
this the two halves of one line are set in two sizes. The row is what the card is created
with, but the spend column is not — until the run names a model there is nothing to report,
and an empty column is still a column, so the button would stand off the left edge as if
something were beside it. The column joins the row with the first line to put in it, which
means the row is replaced whole: see FeishuCardElements.stopButtonRow(). So a deployment
restyling this row has to keep the spend first among the columns.
The rest are added the first time the run has something to put in them rather than sitting
empty on every card: an element the card carries is space the card gives up, and most runs
write no todo list and are interrupted by nobody. 'message' is the answer itself — until the
model says its first word there is nothing to show, and a streaming card says as much for
itself in the chat list. 'queued' holds what the user said
while the run was working, one quoted line per message, and goes above the answer so the card
reads in the order things were said: the message Feishu quotes above the card, then this, then
the reply. 'reasoning' is what the model thought its way through, on an endpoint that reports
it, in a panel of its own between the queued messages and the answer: it is not the answer,
so it is never folded into one. It is added the moment there is thinking to put in it and so
arrives open, because thinking is the only thing happening at that moment and a reader
watching a card do nothing is owed the one thing it is doing. It is folded away again once the
run ends and there is an answer above it to read instead — 'expanded' here is the state it is
born in, not the state it keeps. Once only, and at that one moment: Feishu reports a panel's
chevron to nobody, so anything more often would be overruling a reader's own choice over and
over rather than once, as the thing they were watching stops.
Its first nested element is the one the run streams the thinking into, which is why a
deployment restyling this panel has to keep something there to write to.
It has no border and no padding, unlike a subagent's panel: a subagent is a piece of work with
a beginning and an end, worth drawing a box around, and this is a line the reader opens. So it
reads as the card's own text with a chevron beside it — 'auto_when_fold' is what keeps the
closed line as narrow as its title while the thinking, once opened, still gets the whole width
to wrap in, and 'follow_text' is what puts the chevron beside the title rather than off at the
right edge of a row nothing else fills. The chevron points right while the pane is closed and
turns to point down as it opens, which is what the 90 degrees is: the angle is what the icon is
rotated by when expanded, not the angle it ends at, so an arrow that already points down would
want -180 and this one wants a quarter turn.
'tools' is what the run has done: every tool call the turn made, in a pane under the answer.
Its title names the tool the run is on now, so a closed pane still says what is happening, and
the first thing inside it is that call's input, quoted — a call is something the run asked
for, which is what a quote reads as. Every call before it follows, oldest first, each one a
pane of its own that opens onto what it was given and what came back: a turn can make dozens
of calls and a reader wants one of them, so the trail is a list of titles until they ask for
more. Born open, like 'reasoning' and for the same reason — while the run is calling tools
that is the only thing to watch — and folded away once the run ends and there is an answer to
read instead. Adding a pane to a pane is not something a card element insert can do, so the
run replaces this element whole on every call; a reader who folds it mid-run will see it open
again on the next one, which is the price of keeping the trail.
'tool_call' is one of those inner panes, titled by the tool it called and nothing else, so the
trail reads as a list of what the run used. It is not an element of the card — the run builds one
per call and nests them here — so unlike everything else in this file it is never inserted by
id and carries none.
'todo' is the run's task list, under the answer. 'references' is where the knowledge the run
was given came from, and 'usage' is what the turn has cost, both in the card's footer with
the sources above the spend. They are worth showing because retrieval happens
without the model asking for it and leaves no tool call behind: without them a reader cannot
tell that anything was consulted, let alone what. A turn that retrieved nothing adds no
element rather than an empty one.
Both panel titles are notation-sized, the card's smallest: a closed panel is a line offering
something rather than saying it, and at body size the chevron line competes with the answer
it sits beside. The size lives on the title's markdown rather than on the panel, because it is
the header text being sized and not what the panel holds — the contents carry their own.
It is a closed panel, unlike 'reasoning' which is born open: thinking is the only thing
happening while a run is working and is worth showing unprompted, whereas sources are a
question a reader asks only once they have read the answer. So it arrives as one narrow grey
line with a chevron — 'auto_when_fold' keeps the closed line as short as its title rather than
letting it span the card, and 'follow_text' puts the chevron beside that title instead of off
at the right edge. Like the reasoning panel, its first nested element is what the run writes
into, so a deployment restyling this has to keep something there. This key is ignored.
